overview: Lucca was a small but long-lived state in northwestern Tuscany. Its aristocratic republic gave way to revolutionary governments, a Napoleonic principality and a Bourbon duchy. This map record covers 1650 to 1878, but independent ducal rule ended in 1847. The outline should therefore not be read as an independent Lucca throughout that entire interval. Public water, schools and hospitals reveal another side of its history alongside aristocratic palaces.

periods.title: The later aristocratic republic
periods.summary: An independent republic governed by its established elite.

periods.title: Revolutionary governments and principality
periods.summary: Changing governments preceded the principality of Elisa Bonaparte and Felice Baciocchi from 1805.

periods.title: Restoration and Bourbon duchy
periods.summary: Austrian provisional administration preceded Bourbon rule from 1817.

periods.title: After independent statehood
periods.summary: Tuscany and then unified Italy governed Lucca; the imported map retains the old label.

sections.title: A fortified city becomes a place to stroll

items.text: Work on Lucca’s great Renaissance walls concluded in 1650, at the beginning of this map interval. In the Serchio flood of 1812, closing the city gates helped keep water out. A structure built for military defence acquired an unexpectedly practical role as protection from the river.

In 1818, Lorenzo Nottolini created the first stretch of public promenade on the walls between the Santa Maria and San Paolino bastions. The Caffe delle Mura followed in 1840. Fortifications gradually became a setting for walking and refreshments: the ramparts had acquired a social life.

sections.title: Silk wealth and a family wedding

items.text: Palazzo Mansi’s major renovation of 1686 to 1691 coincided with Carlo Mansi’s marriage to Eleonora Pepoli in 1688. Architect Raffaello Mazzanti helped turn joined older houses into an imposing residence. A family wedding could be an occasion for years of building work, rather than simply a day of celebrations.

The Mansi family traded in silk. Their palace’s alcove preserves a lavish bed and embroidered satin hangings with flowers and colourful birds. These rooms display an elite household’s wealth and the skilled textile work behind it. They should not be mistaken for the usual furnishings of a Lucchese home.

Lucca’s authorities had discussed improving the city’s water supply since the early eighteenth century. Nottolini’s aqueduct finally began in 1823, carrying spring water from Mount Pisano toward public fountains. Work continued with interruptions until 1851, so the project outlasted the independent duchy.

At Guamo, a small neoclassical building collected spring water in a divided basin. The water then travelled over a long line of brick and masonry arches toward San Concordio. This carefully staged route joined collection, storage and delivery in one public system.

The final approach to the city used large iron pipes below ground. As Mazzarosa explained in 1843, joints allowed movement as metal expanded in heat and contracted in cold. Good plumbing had to leave room for a pipe to change length without breaking.

sections.title: Learning and care beyond the palace

items.text: A university-level institution opened in Lucca in 1785, and a chemistry chair with instruments followed in 1790. The educational reform of 1819 brought a botanical garden, an observatory, physics and anatomical collections, and a natural-history museum. Scientific learning involved examining real things as well as reading books.

A decree of 28 February 1837 established free Sunday classes for artisans. Subjects included practical arithmetic, geometry, industrial mechanics and technical chemistry, alongside farming and elementary veterinary knowledge. The programme connected study with workshop and agricultural skills rather than reserving every lesson for future lawyers.

The merchant guild managed San Luca hospital until the guild’s suppression in 1807, when princely government took over its patronage. The complex contained separate wards for men and women and accommodation for foundlings. Its buildings and records show how trade institutions, government and charitable care became intertwined.

Mazzarosa’s 1843 guide reports 110 beds in the hospital’s men’s wards and 137 in the women’s wards, with adjoining rooms for medical and surgical clinical teaching. These are a contemporary visitor’s figures, not a modern measure of care quality. The guide itself asks for further improvements.

An eighteenth-century Lucca soldo in the national cultural-property catalogue carries “LIBERTAS” across its crowned shield. The Latin word means “liberty”. The reverse shows a saint holding the city. This surviving coin connects the republic’s public identity with an object people could handle in daily exchange.

ending.text: In 1847, Duke Carlo Ludovico ceded Lucca to the Grand Duchy of Tuscany, ending its separate statehood. The city, its institutions and its inhabitants continued under a different government. The imported 1878 endpoint is not the duchy’s fall date.
